caveats: One party predominates (district sweep — 4 of 4 district vote shares fall on the Republican side of 0.5, 0 on the other, a minority share of 0 at or below the 0.25 threshold). CRITERIA.md section 5.1 holds that only efficiency_gap, declination should be trusted in this regime; treat mean_median, partisan_bias as unreliable here, whatever their sign says.

One party wins every seat (Republican, 4 of 4), so declination is undefined and returns None (CRITERIA.md section 5.1). The sweep cannot get any wider, so the seats-votes curve is flat on the Republican side of the observed election — but it is not flat through it, and how far it runs before it steps is a fact about this plan and not a general one. Here district 3 sits at 0.498241, so a uniform swing of 0.001759 — 0.18 points of two-party vote share — moves the Democratic seat share from 0 to 0.25. Read the sweep as that margin, not as a structural fact.

Only 4 districts. Declination fits one line through the losing districts and one through the winning ones, so below 8 districts each line rests on a handful of points and the angle it returns is dominated by which side of 0.5 a single district falls on. Partisan bias is quantised to multiples of 0.125 seat share for the same reason (0.0625 where a swing splits a tied district), so it has no resolution below half a seat here.
